posts.title: Designing a Fault-Tolerant EKF for UAVs
posts.excerpt: A deep dive into implementing residual-based fault detection and isolation mechanisms within an Extended Kalman Filter for robust UAV state estimation.
posts.content:
## Introduction

State estimation is the backbone of any autonomous flight system. When sensors fail, the consequences can be catastrophic. In this post, I'll walk through my approach to building a fault-tolerant EKF that can detect, isolate, and recover from sensor failures in real-time.

## The Problem

Traditional EKFs assume all sensors are trustworthy. In reality, GPS dropouts, IMU saturation, and magnetometer interference are common. The challenge is distinguishing between normal noise and actual faults.

## Solution Architecture

The fault-tolerant EKF uses three key mechanisms:

1. **Residual Monitoring**: Each sensor's innovation sequence is monitored for statistical anomalies
2. **Hypothesis Testing**: A bank of EKFs runs in parallel, each excluding one sensor
3. **Graceful Degradation**: When a fault is detected, the system switches to a reduced sensor configuration

## Implementation Details

The residual-based approach uses a chi-squared test on the normalized innovation squared (NIS). When NIS exceeds a threshold for consecutive samples, a fault is declared.

## Results

Testing with 100+ injected fault scenarios showed 95% detection accuracy with <2% false alarm rate. The system maintained safe flight even with complete GPS loss for up to 60 seconds.

## Conclusion

Fault tolerance isn't just about redundancy—it's about intelligent monitoring and rapid adaptation. The techniques discussed here have been validated in flight and are applicable to a wide range of autonomous systems.

posts.title: From SIL to Flight: A Testing Checklist
posts.excerpt: A comprehensive checklist for transitioning control algorithms from simulation to real flight tests, based on lessons learned from multiple UAV projects.
posts.content:
## The Gap Between Simulation and Reality

Every robotics engineer knows the pain: code works perfectly in simulation, fails mysteriously in real flight. After years of debugging crashed drones, I've developed a systematic checklist for this transition.

## Pre-Flight Verification

### 1. Sensor Calibration
- [ ] IMU temperature compensation verified
- [ ] Magnetometer hard/soft iron calibration
- [ ] Barometer noise characterization
- [ ] GPS accuracy assessment in target environment

### 2. Control Loop Validation
- [ ] Step response matches simulation within 10%
- [ ] Gain margins verified with injected noise
- [ ] Saturation handling tested
- [ ] Emergency modes (RTL, Land) validated

### 3. Hardware-in-the-Loop
- [ ] Real-time constraints met (<5ms jitter)
- [ ] Sensor models match real characteristics
- [ ] Actuator dynamics included
- [ ] Fault injection scenarios passed

## First Flight Protocol

1. **Tethered Test**: Verify basic stability with safety line
2. **Hover Test**: 30-second hover with position hold
3. **Waypoint Mission**: Simple box pattern at 10m altitude
4. **Edge Cases**: Max speed, max climb rate, wind handling

## Lessons Learned

The most common failures are timing-related. Always profile your code on the actual flight computer, not your development machine.

posts.title: Tuning MPC for Wind Rejection
posts.excerpt: Practical tips for tuning Model Predictive Controllers to handle wind disturbances in fixed-wing UAV applications.
posts.content:
## Why MPC for Wind?

Model Predictive Control offers inherent advantages for wind rejection: it looks ahead, respects constraints, and can explicitly model disturbances. But tuning it for aerial vehicles requires careful consideration.

## Key Tuning Parameters

### Prediction Horizon
For wind rejection, the horizon must capture the relevant dynamics:
- Fixed-wing: 2-3x the turn radius at cruise speed
- Multirotor: 1-2 seconds of flight time

### Disturbance Model
Adding a wind state to the prediction model significantly improves performance. I use a simple random walk model with appropriate covariance.

### Cost Function Weights
The trade-off between tracking accuracy and control smoothness becomes critical in wind. I recommend:
- High weight on position error
- Moderate weight on velocity error
- Low weight on control rate (for smooth actuation)

## Real-World Results

On a 2kg fixed-wing platform, the tuned MPC reduced cross-track error by 60% in 10 m/s winds compared to a well-tuned PID controller.

## Computational Considerations

MPC on embedded hardware requires careful formulation. Using ACADO Toolkit with code generation, I achieved 50Hz update rate on a Pixhawk 4.

posts.title: Rover Imitation Learning: Lessons Learned
posts.excerpt: Reflections on training end-to-end navigation policies for ground robots from expert demonstrations.
posts.content:
## The Promise of Imitation Learning

Why write complex planners when you can learn from experts? This was the question that started my journey into imitation learning for rover navigation.

## Data Collection

Quality demonstrations are crucial. I used a game controller to drive 50+ hours across varied terrain. Key lessons:

1. **Coverage matters**: Include edge cases (obstacles, tight turns, slopes)
2. **Consistency helps**: Smooth, deliberate driving is easier to learn
3. **Label everything**: Timestamped sensor data enables rich supervision

## Model Architecture

The final architecture was surprisingly simple:
- Input: 224x224 RGB image + current velocity
- Backbone: ResNet-18 (pretrained on ImageNet)
- Output: Steering angle + throttle

## The Distribution Shift Problem

The biggest challenge: the policy encounters states never seen during training. Solutions that worked:

1. **Data augmentation**: Random brightness, contrast, noise
2. **Domain randomization**: Vary simulation parameters
3. **DAgger iterations**: Collect data from the learned policy

## Deployment

Running at 30Hz on Jetson Nano required TensorRT optimization. The final model uses 2GB memory and achieves 15ms inference time.
